request.idea: A desk fan with a USB-C plug and one button

brief.title: USB-C desk fan
brief.understanding: You want a small fan that sits on a desk, gets its power from a USB-C plug, and is operated with a single button. I am assuming the button turns it on and steps through a few speeds, with no battery, app or wireless features.

questions.question: What should the one button do?
questions.why: On/off only needs no controller at all; speed steps need a small microcontroller.

questions.question: Should it run only while plugged in, or also from a built-in battery?
questions.why: A battery adds a charger, protection circuit, cost and size.

questions.question: How large should the fan blade be?
questions.why: Blade size sets airflow, noise and the size of the housing.

questions.question: What kind of fan motor should it use?
options: Bare DC motor with a propeller blade
questions.why: A PC-style fan is quiet, safe and cheap; a bare motor needs a guard and more design work.

questions.question: What is the target parts cost for one unit?
questions.why: Budget decides fan quality and how nice the enclosure can be.

requirements: Power input: USB-C receptacle, 5 V only, with 5.1 kOhm resistors on CC1 and CC2 so USB-C chargers supply power
Current draw: under 500 mA at full speed (under 2.5 W) so it works from any USB port or charger
Fan: 120 mm 5 V brushless fan, roughly 40-60 CFM at full speed
Noise: under 30 dBA at 0.5 m on low speed
Control: one push button cycling off, low (~40%), medium (~70%), high (100%)
Speed control by PWM at about 25 kHz so there is no audible whine
Standby current when off: under 1 mA
Footprint: about 130 x 130 x 60 mm including stand, stable when the button is pressed

blocks.name: Power input
blocks.role: Takes 5 V from a USB-C charger or port and protects against shorts.
blocks.parts: USB-C 2.0 power-only receptacle (e.g. TYPE-C-31-M-12), 2x 5.1 kOhm CC resistors, 500 mA resettable polyfuse, 10 uF input

blocks.name: Logic supply
blocks.role: Drops 5 V to 3.3 V for the microcontroller.
blocks.parts: 3.3 V LDO such as MCP1700-3302 or AP2112K-3.3

blocks.name: Button
blocks.role: Single user input that cycles the fan through off and three speeds.
blocks.parts: 12 mm tactile switch or 6 mm tact switch with cap, 100 nF debounce capacitor

blocks.name: Controller
blocks.role: Reads the button, remembers the speed step and generates the PWM signal.
blocks.parts: RP2040-Zero or ESP32-C3 Super Mini board (an ATtiny85 or CH32V003 also works for a cheaper custom PCB)

blocks.name: Fan driver
blocks.role: Switches fan power on and off rapidly to set the speed.
blocks.parts: Logic-level N-MOSFET such as AO3400, 100 Ohm gate resistor, 10 kOhm pull-down, 1N5819 flyback diode; not needed if a 4-p

blocks.name: Fan
blocks.parts: 120 mm 5 V brushless fan, e.g. Noctua NF-A12x25 5V PWM or a generic 5 V 120 mm USB fan

blocks.name: Enclosure and stand
blocks.role: Holds the fan upright, keeps fingers off the blades and houses the board and button.
blocks.parts: 3D-printed frame with fan grilles on both sides and rubber feet

risks: Without the two 5.1 kOhm CC resistors, USB-C to USB-C chargers will not supply any power; check with both a C-to-C and an A-to-C cable.
Low-side PWM on a 2- or 3-wire brushless fan can cause whine or failure to start at low duty; test the chosen fan's minimum duty, add a brief full-power kick at start, or use a 4-pin PWM fan.
Fan start-up current can exceed its rated current and dip the 5 V rail, resetting the controller; measure inrush and add bulk capacitance (100-220 uF) if needed.
A light fan on a small stand can tip or slide when the button is pressed; place the button low or on the base and add rubber feet or weight.
